# File-type filtering in `ignore`

ripgrep's `-t`/`-T`/`--type-add` filtering lives in the `ignore` crate
(`crates/ignore`), not in the `rg` binary itself. It's a self-contained glob
dispatch table with two halves: a builder (`TypesBuilder`) that accumulates
definitions and selections, and an immutable matcher (`Types`) that the
directory walker consults once per candidate path. Everything described here
is in `crates/ignore/src/types.rs`, with the shipped type list in
`crates/ignore/src/default_types.rs`.

## Representing a type definition

A file type is a `FileTypeDef`: a `name: String` plus `globs: Vec<String>`
(`types.rs:146`). There's no separate "type" identity beyond the name — `rust`
is just whatever globs are currently registered under the key `"rust"`.
`TypesBuilder` holds the working set as `types: HashMap<String, FileTypeDef>`
(`types.rs:306`), keyed by name, so a second `add("rust", "*.rs2")` extends
the existing definition's glob list rather than replacing it.

Definitions arrive three ways:

- `add_defaults()` walks the `DEFAULT_TYPES` table — a hand-maintained,
  `#[rustfmt::skip]` slice of `(&[&str], &[&str])` pairs (aliases, globs) —
  and calls `add()` for every alias/glob pair. A unit test
  (`default_types.rs:335`) asserts the table is sorted lexicographically by
  each entry's first alias, so adding an entry out of order fails `cargo
  test` immediately.
- `add(name, glob)` registers one glob under one name directly. It rejects
  `name == "all"` and any name containing a non-alphanumeric character
  (`Error::InvalidDefinition`), because `"all"` is a reserved selector (see
  below) and type names are matched as plain identifiers on the CLI.
- `add_def(spec)` parses the `--type-add`/`--type-not` string syntax:
  `"name:glob"` (a root definition) or `"name:include:other,names"` (pulls in
  every glob already registered under each listed name and re-adds it under
  `name`). The include form fails fast if any referenced name isn't already
  defined — it does not defer resolution to build time.

Selection is tracked separately from definition. `TypesBuilder.select(name)`
and `.negate(name)` push `Selection::Select`/`Selection::Negate` values
(`types.rs:184`) onto a `selections: Vec<Selection<()>>`; they don't touch the
`types` map. The special name `"all"` expands immediately, at call time, into
one selection per name currently in `self.types.keys()` — so a `select("all")`
only picks up types added *before* it's called, not ones added afterward.
`clear(name)` just removes an entry from the `types` map (`HashMap::remove`),
which is why `--type-clear` only makes sense before any `--type-add` for the
same name in the same invocation.

## Building the matcher

`TypesBuilder::build()` (`types.rs:322`) does the real work: for every
selection, in the order it was pushed, it looks up the definition, feeds each
of its globs into a `globset::GlobSetBuilder` with `literal_separator(true)`,
and records `(selection_index, glob_index)` in a parallel
`glob_to_selection: Vec<(usize, usize)>`. `literal_separator(true)` means `*`
does not cross a `/` — a glob like `*.rs` matches a bare filename, not a path
segment boundary. The result is a single compiled `GlobSet` (`Types.set`)
covering every glob from every selection at once; there is no per-type
sub-matcher.

Order matters here in a way that's easy to miss: `globset::GlobSet` numbers
patterns by insertion sequence and `matches_into` returns matching indices in
ascending order (`crates/globset/src/lib.rs:378`). `Types::matched()`
(`types.rs:261`) takes `matches.last()` as the "highest precedent" hit — i.e.
whichever matching selection was registered *last* wins, which is CLI
argument order, not glob specificity. `-t rust -T rust` and `-T rust -t rust`
therefore disagree on `.rs` files. `builder.build()` is also where
`Error::UnrecognizedFileType` and `Error::Glob` (bad glob syntax) surface —
building is the only fallible step; `add`/`select`/`negate` themselves don't
fail except on a malformed `add`.

`Types::matched(path, is_dir)` returns `Match<Glob>` (`ignore::Match`, shared
with gitignore matching). Directories always get `Match::None` — type globs
never apply to them — and only the file name (via `pathutil::file_name`) is
matched, never the full path. If nothing matched but `has_selected` is true
(at least one non-negated selection exists), the result is `Match::Ignore`
rather than `Match::None`: once you've said `-t rust`, everything that isn't
Rust is implicitly excluded, not merely "not preferred."

## Where it plugs into the walker

`WalkBuilder::types()` forwards a built `Types` into `dir::IgnoreBuilder`
(`crates/ignore/src/dir.rs:666`), which stores it behind an `Arc` and
consults it inside `Ignore::matched()` (`dir.rs:365`). Precedence there is
fixed: `-g`/`--glob` overrides are checked first and short-circuit on any
match; then gitignore-style rules; only if neither ignores the path does the
type matcher get a look. A type match can still whitelist a path that
gitignore rules didn't mention, but it can't override an explicit `-g`
exclusion or a `.gitignore` rule — the flag's own doc comment in
`crates/core/flags/defs.rs` states this explicitly for `-t`/`--type-not`.

## What a contributor needs to know

The CLI wiring is in `crates/core/flags/hiargs.rs::types()`: it calls
`add_defaults()` once, then replays `LowArgs.type_changes` — a
`Vec<TypeChange>` (`Clear`/`Add`/`Select`/`Negate`) built by `defs.rs` in the
exact order `-t`, `-T`, `--type-add`, `--type-clear` appeared on the command
line. Because defaults are added before any user change, `--type-clear` can
remove a default even if it appears last; because changes replay in argument
order, `--type-add 'src:*.foo' --type-clear src` deletes the addition, while
reversing the two flags does not.

Adding a new default type means editing `DEFAULT_TYPES` in
`default_types.rs`, keeping the first alias in lexicographic order (or the
sort test fails), and adding a `matched!`/`matched!(not, ...)` case in
`types.rs`'s test module if the glob has any edge case worth pinning down.
Nothing here reads file contents or extensions beyond what the glob expresses
— a "type" is exactly its glob set, nothing more.
